lessons.title: The principles of integrated pest management
lessons.html:
What is IPM?

Integrated pest management (IPM) is a decision-based approach that combines several methods to keep pests, diseases and weeds below levels that cause economic damage, while protecting people, beneficial organisms and the environment. Chemicals are used only when needed, chosen carefully and applied correctly. South African export industries such as citrus, deciduous fruit and table grapes rely heavily on IPM to meet residue limits and market requirements.

Core principles

  1. Prevention: stop pest problems from developing through crop choice, hygiene and cultural practices.
  2. Identification: know exactly which pest, disease or weed is present, and which organisms are beneficial.
  3. Monitoring: scout regularly and record pest and beneficial numbers.
  4. Thresholds: act only when the pest reaches an action or economic threshold.
  5. Combining methods: use cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical controls together.
  6. Evaluation: check whether controls worked and adjust.

Economic threshold

The economic injury level is the pest density at which the cost of damage equals the cost of control. The economic (action) threshold is set lower so that control is applied before that level is reached. Thresholds are crop- and pest-specific; obtain them from industry bodies, researchers or your crop adviser.

Why not just spray on a calendar?

  • Unnecessary sprays cost money.
  • Broad-spectrum products kill natural enemies, leading to secondary pest outbreaks (for example red mite flaring after some insecticides).
  • Repeated use of one mode of action selects for resistance.
  • Residues can cause market rejections.
  • Worker exposure and environmental contamination increase.

lessons.title: Monitoring and control methods
lessons.html:
Tools in the IPM toolbox

Monitoring

  • Scouting: walk fields in a fixed pattern (e.g. W or zig-zag), inspect a set number of plants and record pests, damage and beneficials.
  • Traps: pheromone traps for moths such as false codling moth or bollworm, yellow sticky traps for whitefly and aphids, fruit fly traps.
  • Weather-based disease models for diseases like late blight or downy mildew.
  • Records: scouting sheets or apps with dates, blocks and counts.

Cultural control

  • Crop rotation to break pest and disease cycles.
  • Resistant or tolerant cultivars and rootstocks.
  • Planting dates that avoid peak pest periods.
  • Field sanitation: removing infested fruit, crop residues and volunteer plants.
  • Balanced fertilisation and irrigation; excess nitrogen can attract sap-sucking pests.

Mechanical and physical control

Hand removal, insect netting in tunnels, fruit bagging, mulches, weeding, traps, and barriers.

Biological control

Natural enemies include predators (ladybirds, lacewings, predatory mites), parasitoid wasps, and pathogens such as Bacillus thuringiensis or entomopathogenic fungi and viruses. Strategies:

  • Conservation: protect existing beneficials by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and providing habitat such as flowering strips.
  • Augmentation: release commercially reared natural enemies.
  • Classical: introduce natural enemies of introduced pests, done only by authorised research bodies.

Chemical control

When thresholds are reached, choose a product registered under Act 36 of 1947 for the crop and target, preferably selective and least harmful to beneficials and bees. Rotate modes of action, follow label rates and pre-harvest intervals, and spray only affected blocks if possible (spot treatment).

lessons.title: Building and evaluating an IPM programme
lessons.html:
Putting IPM into practice

Steps to develop a programme

  1. List key pests, diseases and weeds for each crop, and their natural enemies.
  2. Draw up a seasonal calendar showing when each pest is likely to appear.
  3. Set scouting methods, frequency and thresholds for each.
  4. List preferred control options in order: cultural, biological, selective chemical, broad-spectrum only as last resort.
  5. Plan resistance management with mode of action rotation.
  6. Train scouts and supervisors; check their identification skills.
  7. Keep records of scouting, decisions and applications.

Example: false codling moth in citrus

An integrated programme may combine orchard sanitation (collecting and destroying fallen fruit), monitoring with pheromone traps, mating disruption, release of sterile moths in areas where such programmes operate, biological products such as granulovirus, and registered chemical options when thresholds are exceeded. Sanitation is essential because larvae develop in dropped fruit.

Safety

Even in IPM, chemical applications need full label PPE, correct mixing on a bunded area away from water, and respect for re-entry and pre-harvest intervals. Never eat, drink or smoke while spraying. If someone is poisoned, remove them from exposure, remove contaminated clothing, wash skin with lots of water and get medical help with the label.

Evaluating the programme

  • Pest damage at harvest and pack-out quality.
  • Number of sprays and cost of control per hectare.
  • Residue test results.
  • Trends in beneficial populations.
  • Signs of resistance (control failures).

Review annually and adjust thresholds, timing and methods.

Key points

  • IPM combines prevention, monitoring, thresholds and multiple control methods.
  • Act when pests reach the action threshold, not on a calendar.
  • Protect natural enemies and use biological control.
  • Choose selective, registered products and rotate modes of action.
  • Record, evaluate and improve the programme every season.
